name: Glam Rock

influenced_by: British pantomime and music-hall theatrical tradition

media.title: David Bowie, The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust (1972)

reacts_against: rock music's increasingly serious, denim-and-authenticity-coded late-1960s image, reintroducing theatrical costume, makeup and deliberate artifice as a point of pride rather than embarrassment.
revivals: a visible influence on 1980s new romantic and glam metal styling
article: Glam rock emerged in Britain around 1971 as a direct rebuke to the denim-and-authenticity aesthetic that had come to dominate rock music by the end of the 1960s. David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona — introduced on the 1972 album The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars — pushed the genre's theatrical, androgynous costuming furthest, blending science-fiction concept with makeup and gender presentation that was genuinely transgressive for mainstream rock at the time. Marc Bolan's T. Rex and Roxy Music built parallel, similarly costume-forward versions of the same impulse, all of them drawing loosely on Britain's older music-hall and pantomime theatrical tradition, where exaggerated makeup and costume were an established, respectable stage convention rather than a rock novelty. Glam's embrace of glitter, platform boots and deliberate artifice left a direct mark on 1980s glam metal (a largely American, harder-rock-oriented descendant) and on the UK's new romantic scene, both of which kept glam's theatricality while dropping much of its original gender-bending edge.
